questions.problem: Expressed as a fraction in its simplest form, ${4}^{-4}=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the reciprocal of the base $(4),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(+4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{-4} & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4})\times (\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1\times 1\times 1\times 1}{4\times 4\times 4\times 4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{256}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Express $\frac{9}{4}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write $\frac{9}{4}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4} & =\frac{3\times 3}{2\times 2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\times \frac{3}{2} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $(\frac{3}{2}),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}={(\frac{2}{3})}^{-2}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Express $\dfrac {1} {49}$ as a base raised to a negative exponent.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write $\dfrac{1}{49}$ as a base raised to a power:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{49} & =\frac{1\times 1}{7\times 7} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\times \frac{1}{7} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{7})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the reciprocal of the base $\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right),$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $(-2),$ as follows:

$$
\left( \dfrac{1}{7} \right)^2 = 7^{-2}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We know how to find $2^{-1}.$ But what about $2^{-2}, 2^{-3},2^{-4},\ldots$?

To work out ${\color{blue}{2}}^{{\color{red}{-2}}},$ all we need to do is find the reciprocal of the base $({\color{blue}{2}})$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the *opposite* sign $({{\color{red}{+2}}})$.

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-2} & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\times (\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{1\times 1}{2\times 2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

A similar approach can be used for other powers. Let's see another example.
